titleStmt.title: Resource Augmentation Bounds for Approximate Demand Bound Functions

analytic.title: Resource Augmentation Bounds for Approximate Demand Bound Functions

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In recent work, approximation of the demand bound function for a sporadic task uses a linear approximation when the interval length of interest is larger than the relative deadline of the task. Such an approximation leads to a factor 2 for resource augmentation under a naïve analysis, i.e., if the schedulability test using this approximate demand bound function fails, the task set is not schedulable by slowing down the system to 50% of the original speed. In this paper we provide a tighter analysis of such an approach on uniprocessor systems and on identical multiprocessor systems with partitioned scheduling under the earliestdeadline-first strategy. For uniprocessor systems, we prove that the resource augmentation factor is at most 2e-1 e ≈ 1.6322, where e is the Euler number. For identical multiprocessor systems with M processors, with respect to resource augmentation, we show that deadline-monotonic partitioning with approximate demand bound functions leads to a factor 3e-1 e -1 M ≈ 2.6322 -1 M for constrained-deadline task sets and a factor 3 -1 M for arbitrarydeadline task sets, in which the best results known so far are 3 -1 M for constrained-deadline ones and 4 -2 M for arbitrarydeadline ones. Moreover, we also provide concrete input instances to show that the lower bound of resource augmentation factors for uniprocessor systems (identical multiprocessor systems under an arbitrary order of fitting and a large number of processors, respectively) under such approaches is 1.5 (2.5, respectively).

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The sporadic task model has been widely adopted in the real-time systems domain [13]. In the sporadic task model, a task τ i is characterized by its relative deadline D i , its minimum inter-arrival time T i , and its (worst-case) execution time C i . For historical reasons, the minimum inter-arrival time is also referred to as the period of the task. A sporadic task is an infinite sequence of task instances, referred to as jobs, where two consecutive jobs of a task should arrive no shorter than the minimum inter-arrival time separation. When a job of task τ i arrives at the system at time t, its absolute deadline is set to t + D i , in which the job should finish no later than its absolute deadline. A (sporadic) task set consists of several sporadic tasks. A task set T is said feasible on a system if there exists a feasible schedule that ensures the timing satisfaction of all the jobs. To test for timing satisfaction, the schedulability test (analysis) for a scheduling policy is to verify whether a (sporadic) task set can meet its timing constraints.

To feasibly schedule a preemptive task set on a uniprocessor system, earliest-deadline-first (EDF) policy has been shown to be optimal [12], in which the job with the earliest absolute deadline has the highest priority for execution. That is, a task set is feasible if and only if the schedule by applying EDF does not violate any timing constraints. For a task set T with implicit deadlines, in which the relative deadline of a task is equal to its minimum inter-arrival time for each sporadic task in T, the schedulability test of EDF is to verify whether the total utilization τi∈T Ci Ti is at most 100% [12], in which the utilization of task τ i is defined as Ci Ti . However, the periodicity and the relative deadline requirements need not necessarily be the same. When the relative deadline of a task is no more than its minimum inter-arrival time for every sporadic task, such a task set is said to have constrained deadlines. If the relative deadline of a sporadic task in a task set is more than its minimum inter-arrival time, such a task set is said to have arbitrary deadlines.

Even though EDF is optimal for schedulability, how to verify the schedulability of EDF is not an easy problem for task sets with constrained deadlines or arbitrary deadlines, as the problem has been shown to be coN P -hard [8]. To provide an exact schedulability test, Baruah et al. [5] show that the most critical instance is to release the first job of tasks synchronously (says, at time 0), and the subsequent job arrivals should be as rapidly as legally possible. Based on that observation, the demand bound function dbf (τ i , t), as in [5], of a task τ i within any time interval with length equal to t (or from time 0 to time t, under the above synchronous release) can be defined as the maximum demand of task τ i to be released and finished in the interval. That is,
div.formula: dbf (τ i , t) = max 0, t -D i T i + 1 × C i . (1
div.p: However, as the demand bound function is not a continuous function, the schedulability test by verifying the summation of the demand bound functions of all the tasks for all t ≥ 0 requires pseudo-polynomial time in the worst case.

To reduce the time complexity for schedulability test, approximations on the demand bound function in (1) have been proposed by Chakraborty et al. [6] and Albers and Slomka [1], [2]. Their approaches take only a constant number, depending on the required approximation precision, of discrete points in the demand bound function of a task and approximate the rest with a linear function.

Moreover, in modern computing systems, multiprocessor platforms have been adopted to accommodate the high computation requirement. For scheduling sporadic tasks on multiprocessor systems, there are three alternatives paradigms: partitioned, global, and semi-partitioned scheduling. The partitioned scheduling approach partitions tasks statically among the available processors. That is, each task is statically assigned to a processor to execute all the jobs of the task on the processor. The global scheduling approach allows a job to be migrated from one processor to another. The semi-partitioned scheduling approach decides whether a task is divided into subtasks statically and each task/subtask is then assigned to a processor statically. A comprehensive survey of multiprocessor scheduling in real-time systems can be found in [7] by Davis and Burns. This paper focuses on partitioned scheduling, which has been shown N P-hard in the strong sense [13]. For task sets with implicit deadlines, the problem is equivalent to the Makespan problem [10], in which the objective is to minimize the maximum utilization among the processors after task partitioning. Therefore, the largest-utilization-task-first strategy proposed in [10] leads to 4 3 -approximation, in which the maximum utilization among the processors by using the strategy is at most 4 3 times of the optimal solution. Specifically, Hochbaum and Shmoys [11] provide a polynomial-time approximation scheme.

For task sets with constrained deadlines or arbitrary deadlines on multiprocessor systems, one safe approach is to transform to a task with an implicit deadline by setting both relative deadline and the minimum inter-arrival time to the minimum of these two parameters, and, then, the schedulability test and partitioning strategy for implicit-deadline task sets can be applied. Unfortunately, this may lead to a very bad task partition, as the task transformation increases too much pessimism.

Baruah and Fisher [3] provide the first non-trivial solution for partitioned scheduling on identical multiprocessor systems when arbitrary-or constrained-deadlined task sets are considered. The problem, of course, is still N P-hard in the strong sense. Baruah and Fisher [3], [4] propose to use deadline-monotonic task partitioning by using the approximate demand bound function proposed by Albers and Slomka in [1]. Specifically, the demand bound function in (1) of task τ i for a given t is approximated by taking a linear approximation when t is larger than the relative deadline D i . By considering tasks iteratively from the shortest relative deadline for task assignment, the deadline-monotonic partitioning algorithm assigns the task under consideration to a processor which is EDF schedulable when using the approximate demand bound function for the schedulability test. Moreover, Fisher also discusses the difficulty associated with partitioned scheduling of sporadic real-time tasks in [9].

Baruah and Fisher prove that deadline-monotonic partitioning based on the approximate demand bound functions for task partitioning has a 4 -2 M (respectively, 3 -1 M ) resource augmentation factor for arbitrary-deadline (constrained-deadline, respectively) task sets [3], [4], where M is the number of processors. That is, for a ρ resource augmentation factor of an algorithm A for the studied problem, it guarantees that If a sporadic task set is feasible on M identical processors, the task partition derived from the algorithm A is feasible on each processor by speeding up to ρ times as fast as in the original platform (speed). The analysis in [3], [4] is based on the observation that the approximate demand bound function leads to a 2-approximation for any t ≥ 0, which is tight with respect to the approximation on the demand bound function. However, it is not tight when considering resource augmentation, which will be explained in detail in Section II-E.

This paper focuses on the improvement of the analysis to show that deadline-monotonic partitioning with the approximate demand bound functions, indeed, has a tighter resource augmentation factor than the above factors provided in [3], [4]. As a basis of the analysis, in this paper, we first prove that the resource augmentation factor for the above approximate demand bound function is at most 2e-1 e ≈ 1.6322, where e is the Euler number. For identical multiprocessor systems, we show that the resource augmentation factor is 3e-1 e

M for task sets with constrained deadlines and 3 -1 M for task sets with arbitrary deadlines. For the lower bound on the resource augmentation factor of the deadlinemonotonic partitioning approach with approximate demand bound functions, we provide input instances to show that the analytical lower bound of the resource augmentation factor for the above approach on uniprocessor systems (identical multiprocessor systems with a large number of processors under non-specified fitting preference, respectively) is 1.5 (2.5, respectively).

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section II specifies the task and platform model and provides the preliminary results in the literature. Section III provides the input instances for the lower bound of the resource augmentation factor for deadline-monotonic partitioning. Section IV focuses on the special case for uniprocessor systems, as the basis of the analysis. Section V gives the resource augmentation analysis for multiprocessor systems. Section VI concludes the paper with an outline of possible future research.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODELS AND PRELIMINARY RESULTS
div.p: This section provides the task and platform model used in this paper, reviews the deadline-monotonic partitioning algorithm proposed in [3], [4] for completeness, and gives the definition of resource augmentation.

div.head: A. Task and Platform Model
div.p: We consider a set T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ N } of N independent sporadic real-time tasks. A task τ i is characterized by its relative deadline D i , its minimum inter-arrival time T i , and its (worst-case) execution time C i . The execution platform has M identical processors, and a task has the same execution and timing property on all of these M processors. We denote the utilization of task τ i as u i = Ci Ti , and the density of task τ i as
div.formula: δ i = Ci min{Ti,Di} .
div.p: Note that, for the rest of this paper, we index the tasks from the shortest relative deadline to the longest, i.e., D i ≤ D j if i < j. A task set T is called an implicit-deadline task set if the relative deadline D i of each task τ i in T is equal to its minimum inter-arrival time T i . A task set T is called a constrained-deadline task set if the relative deadline D i of each task τ i in T is no more than its minimum inter-arrival time T i . A task set T is called an arbitrary-deadline task set if there exists a task τ i in T with relative deadline D i larger than its minimum inter-arrival time T i .

div.head: E. Resource Augmentation
div.p: If Algorithm 1 returns a feasible task assignment, all the tasks are guaranteed to meet the timing constraints since the dbf * function over-approximates the dbf function. Note that, if dbf * is replaced by dbf in (5) when Algorithm 1 is applied, the resulting task partition may not be feasible even though
div.formula: C i + τj ∈Tm dbf (τ j , D i ) ≤ D i holds.
div.p: The main issue here is to answer what can be guaranteed when Algorithm 1 returns failure in task partitioning. The resource augmentation technique helps quantify such failure, which provides the worst-case guarantees.

If an algorithm A for the studied problem has a ρ resource augmentation factor, it guarantees that the task partition derived from the algorithm A is always feasible on each processor by speeding up to ρ times as fast as in the original platform speed, if task set T is feasible on the original M identical processors. In other words, by taking the negation of the above statement, we know that if the algorithm A fails to feasibly partition the task set T on M identical processors, there is no feasible task partition when each processor runs 1 ρ times slowler than the original platform speed. Baruah and Fisher [3], [4] prove that Algorithm 1 has a 4 -2 M (respectively, 3 -1 M ) resource augmentation factor for arbitrary-deadline (constrained-deadline, respectively) task sets.

Note that the above theorems on lower bounds of resource augmentation are based on concrete input instances. Even though the lower bound of the first-fit strategy is lower than the others on multiprocessor systems, we do not claim that the first-fit strategy has a better worst-case resource augmentation factor than others. The gap between these lower bounds stems from the difficulty in identifying a set of concrete input instances for the first-fit strategy.

The lower bounds provided here are different from the lower bound 2 -2 M provided in Theorem 1 in [9], which comes from the resource augmentation by comparing the partitioned scheduling to the global scheduling. The lower bounds provided here are for specific fitting strategies with comparison to feasible partitioned scheduling. In fact, there does not exist any feasible partitioned schedule for the task set provided in Theorem 1 in [9] at the original speed. Therefore, by the definition of the resource augmentation factor in this paper, that instance has a resource augmentation factor 1, in which the feasibility of a schedule is defined by partitioned scheduling.

div.head: VI. CONCLUDING REMARKS
div.p: This paper studies the resource augmentation factor for the deadline-monotonic partitioning algorithm proposed by Baruah and Fisher in [3], [4], in which the approximate demand bound function in (3) is used for efficiently determining whether a task can be feasibly assigned to one processor.

We first present concrete input instances, in which the analytical lower bound of the resource augmentation factor for uniprocessor systems is 1.5. For identical multiprocessor systems with M processors, when the first-fit strategy is used for task assignment, the analytical lower bound for the resource augmentation factor is 2 -2 M +1 , while the worst-fit strategy or the random-fit strategy has an analytical lower bound

. When M is sufficiently large, the corresponding lower bounds above are 2 and 2.5. For the upper bound on the resource augmentation factor, we show that it is at most 2e-1 e ≈ 1.6322 for uniprocessor systems, at most 3e-1 e -1 M ≈ 2.6322 -1 M for constrained-deadline sporadic task sets on identical multiprocessor systems, and 3-1 M and for arbitrary-deadline sporadic task sets on identical multiprocessor systems.

Even though we focus ourself on resource augmentation by comparing to (feasible) partitioned scheduling, because the statement in Lemma 1 also holds for global scheduling and optimal global scheduling is superior to partitioned scheduling, the upper and lower bounds of the resource augmentation factors provided here are also correct when comparing to optimal global scheduling. However, by Theorem 1 in [9], the resource augmentation of partitioned scheduling is at least 2 -2 M against global scheduling. The instance provided in Theorem 3 is not representative any more. For future research, we would like to tighten the analysis, and consider uniform multiprocessor systems. It would also be interesting to exploit fine-grained approximation schemes, as in [1], [6], for designing task partitioning algorithms with better resource augmentation factors.
